title: Motion, Its Types, and Force
summary: Rest and motion, the five types of motion, and what a force is, with its effects and kinds.

p: Motion is a change in the position of a body with time, measured from a fixed reference point. A body is at rest if its position does not change with time. A body is in motion if its position changes with time.
Rest and motion are relative. A passenger sitting still in a moving bus is at rest compared with the seat but in motion compared with a tree by the roadside.
Translational motion: movement of the whole body from one place to another along a straight or curved path.
Linear motion: a kind of translational motion along a straight line (a car on a straight road, a falling stone).
Rotational motion: the body spins about an axis (a ceiling fan, the wheels of a bicycle).
Oscillatory (vibratory) motion: back-and-forth movement about a fixed point (a pendulum, a guitar string).
Circular motion: movement along a circle (the Moon going round the Earth).
Random motion: irregular, unpredictable movement (smoke particles, gas molecules).

img.alt: Five panels showing linear motion, curvilinear motion, circular motion, rotational motion and oscillatory motion

p: A force is a push or a pull that can start, stop or change the motion of a body, or change its shape. Force is a vector quantity, so it has size and direction. The SI unit is the newton (N).
Force = mass x acceleration, or F = ma. A force of 1 N gives a mass of 1 kg an acceleration of 1 m/s².
Example: what force gives a 4 kg trolley an acceleration of 3 m/s²? F = 4 x 3 = 12 N.
Start or stop a motion (kicking a stationary ball; a goalkeeper stopping it).
Change the direction of an object (a hockey stick turning the ball).
Change the speed of an object (pressing the accelerator).
Change the shape or size of an object (squeezing a sponge, stretching a spring).
Contact forces need the objects to touch: applied force, friction, tension in a rope, normal reaction from a surface, and air resistance.
Non-contact (field) forces act across a distance: gravitational force, magnetic force and electrostatic force.

activity: Walk around your home or school for five minutes. List one example of each type of motion (linear, rotational, oscillatory, circular, random) and say which force is causing it.

title: Friction
summary: What friction is, its types, advantages, disadvantages, how to increase or reduce it, and a worked calculation.

p: Friction is a force that opposes the movement, or the tendency to move, of two surfaces in contact. It always acts in the direction opposite to the motion. Rub your two palms together quickly: the warmth you feel is caused by friction.
Static friction is the force that must be overcome to start a body moving. It acts on a body that is not moving yet.
Kinetic (dynamic) friction acts on a body that is already sliding. Static friction is greater than kinetic friction, which is why it is harder to get a heavy box moving than to keep it moving.

The size of the friction force depends on how rough the surfaces are and how hard they press together: F = μN, where μ (mu) is the coefficient of friction (it has no unit) and N is the normal reaction, the force with which the surface pushes up on the body. On a flat floor N = mg.
It lets us walk and drive without slipping.
It makes the brakes of vehicles work.
It lets us grip and hold tools.
It lets belts and pulleys work in machines.
It wears out machine parts and tyres.
It wastes energy as heat.
It lowers the efficiency of moving parts.
It makes moving heavy objects harder.
To reduce friction: use oil or grease (lubrication), polish the surfaces, use ball bearings or rollers, and give vehicles and aircraft a streamlined shape.
To increase friction: use rough surfaces, increase the weight pressing down, put treads on tyres, and wear rubber-soled shoes.

p: A box of mass 5 kg is pulled along a horizontal floor with a force of 30 N. The coefficient of kinetic friction between the box and the floor is 0.2. Find the acceleration of the box. (g = 9.8 m/s²)

b: Normal reaction N = mg = 5 x 9.8 = 49 N.
Acceleration a = net force / mass = 20.2 / 5 = 4.04 m/s².

title: Equations of Motion
summary: The three equations for uniform acceleration, where they come from, and worked examples.

p: The equations of motion are three formulas that link five quantities: u (initial velocity), v (final velocity), a (acceleration), t (time) and s (displacement). They work only when the acceleration is uniform (constant) and the motion is in a straight line.
Start with the definition of acceleration: a = (v - u) / t. Rearranging gives the first equation: v = u + at.
For uniform acceleration, the average velocity is (u + v) / 2. Distance = average velocity x time, so s = ((u + v) / 2) x t. Replacing v with u + at gives the second equation: s = ut + ½at².
Finally, remove t between the first two equations to get the third: v² = u² + 2as.
Learn them by heart. Choose the one that has the quantity you want and the quantities you know.

p: A car accelerates uniformly from rest at 2 m/s² for 10 s. Find (a) its final velocity and (b) the distance covered.

b: (b) s = ut + ½at² = 0 + ½ x 2 x 10² = ½ x 2 x 100 = 100 m.

p: A body with an initial velocity of 12 m/s accelerates at 3 m/s² for 4 s. Final velocity v = 12 + 3 x 4 = 24 m/s. Distance s = 12 x 4 + ½ x 3 x 16 = 48 + 24 = 72 m.
A car takes off from rest and covers 80 m in 10 s. Use s = ut + ½at² with u = 0: 80 = ½ x a x 100, so a = 1.6 m/s².

title: Free Fall and Gravity
summary: Motion under gravity: objects thrown upwards, dropped, or thrown horizontally, with worked examples.

p: When an object is thrown upwards or released from a height and only gravity acts on it, it is in free fall. Near the surface of the Earth, gravity gives every falling object the same acceleration, g = 9.8 m/s² (about 10 m/s²), downwards. A heavy stone and a light stone dropped together reach the ground together if air resistance is small. In the equations of motion we simply replace a with g.

When an object moves upwards, gravity slows it down, so a = -g. The equations of motion become: v = u - gt, h = ut - ½gt² and v² = u² - 2gh. When an object falls downwards, gravity speeds it up, so a = +g and we use v = u + gt, h = ut + ½gt² and v² = u² + 2gh.
At the highest point of its flight, an object thrown upwards has v = 0 for an instant. The time to rise to the top is t = u / g and the greatest height is h = u² / 2g.

sections.h: Worked example 1: a ball thrown upwards
p: A ball is thrown upwards at 20 m/s. Find (a) the time it takes to reach its highest point and (b) the greatest height. Take g = 10 m/s².

b: u = 20 m/s, v = 0 at the top, g = 10 m/s².
(a) v = u - gt gives 0 = 20 - 10t, so t = 2 s.
(b) v² = u² - 2gh gives 0 = 400 - 20h, so h = 20 m.
The ball takes another 2 s to fall back, so the total time of flight is 4 s.

sections.h: Worked example 2: a stone dropped from a height
p: A stone is dropped from the top of a tower 45 m high. How long does it take to hit the ground, and how fast is it moving when it lands? (g = 10 m/s²)

b: h = ½gt² gives 45 = 5t², so t² = 9 and t = 3 s.

p: A particle is thrown horizontally at 10 m/s from the top of a tower 20 m high. Find the horizontal distance travelled before it hits level ground. (g = 10 m/s²)

b: The vertical motion and the horizontal motion are independent. Downwards: initial vertical velocity = 0, h = 20 m.
h = ½gt² gives 20 = 5t², so t² = 4 and t = 2 s.
Horizontally the velocity stays 10 m/s (no force acts sideways).

activity: Drop a small stone from the height of your shoulder and time its fall with a phone stopwatch (it will be very short). Then measure your shoulder height and use h = ½gt² to find t, and compare it with your measured time.
